cultivar: Lingtou Dancong (Bai Ye), a Fenghuang Shui Xian selection
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted, traditionally to a medium level that brings its honey aroma forward.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April, early because the cultivar sprouts early and the gardens are lower), with autumn and winter pickings; spring is the quality harvest.
appearance_dry: Long, slightly loose, yellowish-brown strips with a honey smell.
appearance_wet: Long, pale yellow-green leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: Honey first and last, with a soft floral note, a medium body, a toasty sweetness and a clean, moderately long finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. A forgiving dancong that also works in a pot, 4 g per 200 ml for a minute; the honey note is clearest in steeps two to four.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and season, spring from May, with autumn and winter (xue pian) lots sold fresh; lightly roasted lots are best within a year, medium roasts keep two to three years sealed and dry. Raoping also sells aged Lingtou Dancong, typically five to ten years old, with the year stated.
description:
Lingtou Dancong is the honey-scented oolong of Lingtou village in Raoping county, the dancong district east of the Fenghuang Mountains, and it is unusual in being both a place and a cultivar: the plant found there in the 1960s now carries the village's name and is grown across Chaozhou and beyond.

The story is well documented by dancong standards. Between 1961 and 1963 growers from Lingtou, in Fubin town, found the plant in their gardens on the slopes of Shuangji Niang mountain and trialled it successfully; it was noted for pale leaves, early sprouting and a strong honey aroma, and over the following decades it became the dominant plant of the area. The Ministry of Agriculture named it Lingtou Dancong in 1981, it is now a national cultivar with the honey type (mi xiang) as its defining character, and the tea carries a protected name. The same plant is also called Bai Ye, white leaf.

It is made the dancong way, sun-withered, shaken through the night, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted, and Lingtou makers traditionally roast to a medium level, which suits the cultivar: the fire deepens the honey and the leaf has no fragile perfume to lose. The cup is golden-orange, the aroma is honey with a soft floral edge, the body is medium with a toasty sweetness, and the finish is clean and moderately long.

Brew it with the Chaozhou method and it gives seven good steeps; brew it in a pot and it makes an easy, honeyed daily oolong. It is more forgiving than the high-mountain strains and a good tea to learn fast pouring on.

It is sold by year and season, spring from May, with winter xue pian lots in December that are lighter and very fragrant, and Raoping shops also sell aged lots from five to ten years old that turn plummy and smooth. It is inexpensive and honest under its own name; the only caution is that it is also sold under grander names, so a Lingtou Dancong priced as Wudong tea is simply mislabelled.
history:
Lingtou Dancong takes its name from Lingtou village in Fubin town, Raoping county. Growers there found the plant on the slopes of Shuangji Niang mountain between 1961 and 1963 and trialled it successfully. Local records say the Ministry of Agriculture gave it the name Lingtou Dancong in 1981, and that it won a national quality title in 1986.

Some local accounts also trace the tea to the Qing dynasty, three centuries back. That sits awkwardly with the 1960s find and probably refers to tea growing in the area rather than to this plant.

Chinese sources report it as a national cultivar with a protected name, and Raoping remains its main home.
